name: Financial Services Use Case
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Where Banks Actually Use Blockchain, and Where They Gave Up
lesson.summary: Financial services has the resources to run blockchain experiments at scale, and its record includes one of the clearer examples of a production deployment (interbank settlement) alongside some of the most visible collapses, including a multi-bank trade finance consortium and Facebook's Diem stablecoin.
lesson.body:
Financial services was an obvious early target for blockchain, because moving money and reconciling records between institutions that do not fully trust each other is close to the exact problem the technology was designed to address. It is worth being precise about scope here: this chapter is about banks and financial institutions building or joining permissioned, enterprise blockchain systems for their own operations, not about public cryptocurrency speculation, which is a separate topic.

JPMorgan built one of the more durable examples. The bank developed Quorum, a permissioned blockchain platform derived from Ethereum, and used it to launch JPM Coin in 2019, a system for settling payments between JPMorgan's own institutional clients around the clock rather than waiting on traditional banking hours and correspondent banking delays. That work was later organized under a division called Onyx, which has also used distributed ledger technology for intraday repurchase agreement (repo) transactions. JPMorgan eventually sold the ongoing development of Quorum to Consensys in 2020 while continuing to use the technology internally. It is fair, and important for a skeptic, to note the tradeoff here directly: because this system mostly runs between JPMorgan and its own institutional clients rather than among a broad set of mutually independent competitors, critics reasonably point out that it functions closer to a private database with cryptographic trimmings than to a public, trust-minimizing blockchain in the fullest sense. That does not make it fake or useless, but it does mean the "decentralized trust among strangers" pitch was never really the point of this particular deployment.

Trade finance consortiums tell a less happy story. we.trade, backed by a group of major European banks including HSBC and Deutsche Bank, launched around 2018 to digitize trade finance paperwork for small and medium-sized businesses, and a competing consortium called Marco Polo pursued similar goals. we.trade ceased operations around 2022. The underlying problem was real, trade finance genuinely involves mountains of paper moving between banks that do not trust each other by default, but the governance challenge was the same one that sank TradeLens in the previous chapter: getting a group of competing banks to commit real, ongoing investment to shared infrastructure is difficult even when everyone agrees the underlying business problem is worth solving.

The clearest example anywhere in financial services of a project failing for reasons that had nothing to do with the technology is Diem, originally announced by Facebook in 2019 as Libra. The plan was a global stablecoin, backed by a basket of major currencies, issued and governed by a Switzerland-based association of large companies. The reaction from regulators and central banks worldwide was immediate and severe, driven by concern that a private company issuing something that functioned like a global currency substitute posed a threat to monetary sovereignty and financial stability. Several of the association's founding members, including PayPal, Visa, Mastercard, eBay, and Stripe, withdrew before the project even launched, in late 2019. The project was renamed Diem in 2020 in an attempt to distance itself from the controversy, and it was ultimately wound down in early 2022, with its remaining technology and assets sold to Silvergate Bank. The core cryptography and engineering behind Diem were largely functional; what killed it was that its ambition collided directly with the authority of national governments over their own currencies, a limitation no amount of good engineering could have addressed.

Taken together, financial services shows blockchain succeeding in narrow, high-trust settings, typically a single large institution and its own clients, and failing in broader, multi-competitor settings or anywhere the project starts to resemble competition with sovereign money. That pattern will come back explicitly in the chapter on what separates successful blockchain adoption from failed adoption.
